guide.title: Unit 8: Cold War and Decolonization: review guide
guide.intro: After 1945, the United States and the Soviet Union competed for global influence without fighting each other directly, while dozens of colonies in Asia and Africa won independence. This unit covers the Cold War's causes and effects, the spread of communism, decolonization and new states, movements that challenged established power, and the end of the Cold War.

sections.title: The Cold War and its end
body: World War II left the United States and the Soviet Union as rival superpowers with opposing systems: capitalist democracy and communist one-party rule. The United States pursued containment through the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan (1947–1948) and formed NATO (1949); the Soviet bloc formed the Warsaw Pact (1955). A nuclear arms race followed.

Because nuclear war threatened both sides, the superpowers fought through proxy wars, as in Korea (1950–1953) and Vietnam, and competed for influence in newly independent states. The Cold War ended as Soviet economic weakness, Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost and perestroika), and the 1989 revolutions in Eastern Europe led to the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.
points: Name both internal and external causes for the end of the Cold War.

sections.title: The spread of communism
body: Communist movements promised land reform and an end to exploitation, which appealed to peasants and workers. In China, Mao Zedong's Communists won the civil war in 1949 with strong peasant support. The Great Leap Forward (1958–1962) caused a famine that killed tens of millions, and the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) persecuted millions more.

Communism also spread through anticolonial struggles: Ho Chi Minh combined nationalism and communism in Vietnam, and Fidel Castro took power in Cuba in 1959, which led to the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962.
points: Land reform was a key appeal of communist movements.
Many movements mixed nationalism with communism.

sections.title: Decolonization and new states
body: Some colonies won independence through negotiation and mass nonviolent protest, as in India under Gandhi and the Indian National Congress (1947) and Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah (1957). Others fought wars, especially where many European settlers lived, as in Algeria (1954–1962) and Kenya.

Independence brought new challenges: the partition of British India into India and Pakistan (1947) caused mass migration and violence, and borders drawn by colonizers often split or combined ethnic groups. Many new states joined the Non-Aligned Movement, launched after the Bandung Conference (1955). Movements against apartheid in South Africa and against Soviet control in Eastern Europe challenged established power.
points: Compare negotiated and violent paths to independence.
Colonial borders and economies shaped new states long after independence.

example.prompt: Explain why decolonization in Algeria was more violent than in Ghana.
example.solution: Algeria had a large population of French settlers and France considered it part of France, so it fought to keep it, leading to a long war; Ghana had few settlers, and Britain negotiated independence with Nkrumah's movement.

misconceptions: The superpowers avoided direct war but backed many deadly proxy wars.
“All new states sided with a superpower.”
Many joined the Non-Aligned Movement to avoid choosing a side.
Some colonies won independence by negotiation; others through long wars.
Many communist movements, as in China, Vietnam, and Cuba, grew from local revolutions.

passages.title: Source A: President Ronald Reagan, speech, March 1983
text: “I intend to do everything I can to persuade [the Soviet Union] of our peaceful intent. [. . .] At the same time, however, they must be made to understand: we will never compromise our principles and standards. We will never give away our freedom. . . . let us be aware that while they preach the supremacy of the State, declare its omnipotence over individual man, and predict its eventual domination of all peoples on the earth, they are the focus of evil in the modern world.”
passages.attribution: Ronald Reagan, President of the United States, speech to the National Association of Evangelicals, March 8, 1983. The bracketed words are OpenStax's. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax World History, Volume 2, section 14.5.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (a speech given by the President in his official role, which is a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax World History, Volume 2 (openstax.org/books/world-history-volume-2/pages/14-5-a-new-world-order); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: An interpretation of paths to independence
text: “In India, Mohandas Gandhi led campaigns of nonviolent civil disobedience, such as the 1930 Salt March, that drew millions into the movement for independence. Britain left in 1947, but it partitioned the subcontinent into a mostly Hindu India and a mostly Muslim Pakistan. Millions of people fled across the new borders, and hundreds of thousands were killed. In Africa, paths differed. In the Gold Coast, Kwame Nkrumah's mass party won elections, and the colony became independent Ghana in 1957 after negotiations. In Algeria, where about a million French settlers lived, the struggle became a war that lasted from 1954 to 1962. Many new states later declared themselves non-aligned in the Cold War.”

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of the spread of communism in Asia and the Americas
text: “Communist parties won their greatest victories not in industrial Europe, as Marx had expected, but among peasants. In China, Mao Zedong's Communists promised land to the poor and defeated the Nationalists in 1949. Mao's Great Leap Forward, an attempt to industrialize rapidly through vast communes, caused a famine that killed tens of millions. In Vietnam, Ho Chi Minh led a movement that fought first French colonial rule and then a U.S.-backed government, combining nationalism with communism. In 1959, Fidel Castro's revolutionaries took power in Cuba. When the Soviet Union placed nuclear missiles on the island in 1962, the world came closer to nuclear war than ever before.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of the Cold War in Europe and beyond
text: “After 1945, Soviet-backed communist governments took power across Eastern Europe. The United States responded with containment. Through the Marshall Plan it gave billions of dollars to rebuild Western European economies, and in 1949 it formed the NATO military alliance; the Soviet Union answered with the Warsaw Pact in 1955. Because both sides came to possess nuclear weapons, they avoided fighting each other directly. Instead they backed opposing sides in wars such as the Korean War of 1950 to 1953. Meanwhile, people around the world challenged entrenched power, from Czechoslovaks during the 1968 Prague Spring to the activists who fought apartheid in South Africa.”
